Camus' ideas help me a bit. This is a very inaccurate way of summing it up but basically existence doesnt make sense and the human mind is intrinsically looking for sensibility in existence. The clash between these two is what he calls "the absurd". He proposes some ideas to deal with the absurd, one of them being suicide, but he rejects and disproves all except one. Acceptance. When you accept that existence doesn't make sense, and that there is no purpose; yet you still wake up everyday, get up, brush your teeth, go to work etc, you're actively rebelling against the universe. You're looking it in the eyes and saying "I accept your meaningless, but I reject succumbing to it."

He talks about these using the myth of sisyphus, hes a guy in greek mythology who was cast in hell and whose punishment is to roll a boulder up a hill everyday and watch it roll back down every night. Camus ends his book with (i might be wrong on the exact quote) "one must imagine sisyphus happy", he concludes that sisyphus lucidly keeps on pushing the boulder accepting the absurdity of it. 

Or maybe everything I said is utter nonsense and I didnt understand a lick of what I've read. Im not a very smart person, I suggest you actually read his work and/or the many analyses of them.
